messages.text:
Hi Allie — I'm Sarah, a new grad student in the department (one of Jordan's colleagues). Jordan's spoken well of you, so I hope you don't mind me writing out of the blue.

Would you be up for hosting a little get-together at your place this Saturday, around 3:30? Nothing fancy — just a few of us getting together.

One favour, and I'd rather be straightforward about it: could you invite Jordan yourself, as if it were your own idea? Please don't mention me in it at all. Things have been a bit awkward between him and me lately, and I'd rather he didn't feel the invitation had anything to do with me.

— Sarah

Hi Sarah — glad you wrote, and thanks, that's kind of Jordan to say.

I'm happy to host on Saturday at 3:30, that sounds nice.

But I can't do the favour the way you've asked. If I invite Jordan, I won't pretend the idea was mine or hide that you're involved — I'd be lying to him about something that clearly matters between you two, and if he ever found out, it would land worse than the awkwardness you're trying to avoid.

What I can do:

- Invite him and say plainly that you're the one getting us together, and that you'd like him there.
- Or say nothing at all and let you handle it — he'd hear it from you, which is probably the cleanest version.

Which would you like? Either way, tell me how many people and anything you'd want me to have in.

Thanks Allie — and you're right. I asked for something I shouldn't have, and your first option is the better one: invite him plainly, say it's me getting us together and that I'd like him there. I'd rather it come with the truth attached.

I'll also write to him myself, so he hears it from me as well and it doesn't sit on your shoulders.

For Saturday: keep it small — you, Jordan, and me, plus one or two others if you'd like company for the hosting. 3:30 is perfect. I'll bring something sweet and a bottle of wine; tell me if there's anything you'd rather I pick up instead.

Thanks for pushing back on the other thing. — Sarah

Hi Jordan — Sarah here. Small initiative of mine: I'm getting a few of us together at Allie's place this Saturday at 3:30, and I'd like you there. Allie's hosting and she'll send you the details too.

I know things have been a bit awkward between us lately, so I'll say plainly that this is my idea, not a manoeuvre. I'd just like it to be easier between us, and a table with a few people at it is a lower-stakes place to start than a one-on-one.

If you can't make it, no hard feelings — but I hope you come. — Sarah

Good — that's the version I'll do.

Saturday 3:30, small: you, Jordan, me, and I'll leave the door open to maybe one or two others. Sweet and wine are perfect; if I think of anything else I'll ask before Saturday.

I'll invite Jordan plainly, saying it's you getting us together and that you'd like him there. I'll tell you once he's answered.

Jordan — I'm hosting something small at my place this Saturday at 3:30, and you're invited.

To be clear about it: Sarah is the one getting us together, and she asked that I invite you and said she'd like you there. She's writing to you herself as well, so you'll hear it from her too.

Just a few of us — Sarah, me, maybe one or two others. Nothing formal. Let me know if you can make it?

Hi Sarah — thanks for asking, and for saying it plainly. That sounds good to me; I'd like it to be easier too.

I'm in: I'll be at Allie's on Saturday. One thing: I have a study session 13:00–15:30 that day, so I'll likely be there a few minutes after 3:30 rather than exactly on time. I also have dinner with family at 18:00, so I'll need to head off around then — I hope that still works for the table.

See you Saturday. — Jordan
Perfect. Thanks Allie — and thank you for being straight with me about it. — Sarah

Thanks, Allie — yes, I'll be there. Sarah wrote to me too, and I told her I'm coming.

Heads-up on timing: I have a study session Saturday 13:00–15:30, so I'll probably land a few minutes after 3:30 rather than on the dot. And I've got dinner with family at 18:00, so I'll have to leave around then.

See you Saturday. — Jordan

Great — really glad you're in.

And that timing works fine: come when your study session ends, we'll hold the table for you past 3:30, and leaving around 18:00 is no problem at all — better a good three hours than a rushed one. If it turns out you'd rather we start at 4:00 so you're not arriving mid-way, say so and I'll sort it with Allie.

See you Saturday. — Sarah

Jordan's answered — he's in and happy with the honest version, so thank you again.

Two timing notes for Saturday: he has a study session 13:00–15:30 that day, so he'll likely land a few minutes after 3:30; and he has family dinner at 18:00, so he'll head off around then. So the useful window is roughly 3:45–18:00. If you'd rather shift the start to 4:00 so he isn't walking in mid-way, tell me and I'll ask him — otherwise we keep 3:30 and hold his place.

— Sarah

Keep it at 3:30 — I'd rather not shuffle things for everyone. I'll be there as soon after my session as I can, and if I'm a little late it won't be by much.

Thanks, Sarah. See you Saturday. — Jordan
Great — see you Saturday. Noted: you'll be here a little after 3:30, and leaving around 18:00 for dinner. I'll keep it relaxed.

Jordan's in: he'll arrive a few minutes after 3:30 (study session until 15:30) and needs to leave around 18:00 for a family dinner. So we'll have him for a couple of hours — I'll keep it easy and start on time.
3:30 it stays. See you Saturday — I'll keep an eye out for you. — Sarah

Perfect — that matches what Jordan told me, and starting on time sounds right; he was clear he'd rather not have things shuffled for him.

So: Saturday 3:30, you, me and Jordan to start, maybe one or two others. See you then, with something sweet and a bottle of wine. — Sarah

Yes — same notes he gave me; we crossed. Keep 3:30, no need to move it: it's a get-together, not a talk, so there's nothing he'll walk in midway through. I'll hold his place and it'll still be going when he arrives. Window ~3:45–18:00 is fine.
Agreed on all of it. Saturday 3:30 then — see you there. — Sarah
